title: A turbulence spectrum asks where the energy sits in scale, and whether a model keeps it there
summary: Spectra, structure functions, correlations and increment PDFs are five views of the same question: how is fluctuation energy shared between large and small scales? Each one is read against a reference (a slope, a Gaussian, a zero line) and each has a regime in which the reference does not apply.

media.alt: Log-log plot of radially averaged energy spectrum E(k) against wavenumber k from 1 to about 130. A black DNS curve declines from about 1e-3 at k=1 through a dotted k^-3.03 reference slope to about 1e-11 at the highest k. Two coarse curves (no model, dashed orange; Smagorinsky, green) end near k=15 and lie one to two decades above the DNS at low k.

source.caption: LES energy-spectrum validation, freely-decaying 2D turbulence
source.note: Group explainer: the representative figure is the energy spectrum. The other four figures of the group are the premultiplied spectrum with spectral flux, the second-order structure function, the two-point correlation with integral length scale, and the velocity-increment PDFs. All come from decaying 2D turbulence with a random-phase initial condition; the project text itself calls the PDF result an honest null and the structure-function slope test inconclusive.

source.project_title: Turbulence Closures — From Mixing Length to Data-Driven RANS

read_the_figure.question: Where in scale does the energy live, does the fine reference show the expected power-law range, and does the coarse run with a sub-grid model stay closer to it than the coarse run without?
read_the_figure.axes: x: wavenumber k (log), from the domain scale on the left to the grid cut-off on the right. y: radially averaged kinetic-energy spectrum E(k) (log), so equal vertical distance is an equal ratio. Each curve is one run at one instant, t = 1.0.
look_at: The black curve is the fine reference (N = 256). It runs to k of about 130; the coarse curves stop near k = 15, which is where a 32-point grid runs out of waves.

The dotted line is a fitted power law labelled k^-3.03 against a theory value of k^-3. It is drawn only over the range where the black curve is straight. Judge the slope there, not over the whole curve.

At the right-hand end of the dashed (no model) curve, look for a rise or a pile-up before the cut-off. Energy that cannot cascade to unresolved scales has nowhere to go and accumulates at the last resolved wavenumbers.
Compare the green (with model) and orange dashed (without) curves with the black curve in the range where they overlap. Which one hugs it more closely, and by how much on a log axis?
Look at the vertical gap between the coarse curves and the black curve at k = 1 to 5. A gap that large at the largest scales is not a sub-grid effect; see 'must check'.
read_the_figure.proves: If the fine curve is straight with the theoretical slope over a decade and the modelled coarse curve follows it over the resolved range with less pile-up than the unmodelled one, then the sub-grid model removes energy at the right end of the spectrum. It does not show the model is right in general: one realization, one setting.
if_wrong: Coarse curves lie above the reference everywhere: the normalisation of E(k) differs between runs (for instance an FFT convention that depends on N), or the initial energy differs. Fix the definition before reading anything else.
A pile-up at the highest resolved k with no model, and an excessive drop with the model: the closure is too weak or too dissipative.
A slope that changes with the fitting window: there is no clean power-law range at this Reynolds number and resolution.
must_check: Both runs use the same definition and normalisation of E(k), and the integral of E(k) is the energy (or the figure says what it is).
The fit window for the reference slope is stated or at least visible, and spans about a decade.
A single snapshot is not a statistic: repeat over realizations or time before claiming a rate.
The coarse grid cut-off is marked, so the reader does not read the end of a curve as a physical drop.
In this figure the coarse curves sit far above the black curve at low k. Confirm that is a normalisation choice and not an energy difference.
as_drawn: Values read by eye, about a factor of two.
Reference at k = 1: about 6e-4. Coarse curves at k = 1: about 4e-2, roughly 60 times higher. Both coarse curves overlap each other up to k of about 5.
The no-model curve peaks near k = 9 at about 0.5; the Smagorinsky curve is lower there by about a factor 5, and falls steeply between k = 10 and 15.
The dotted fit passes from about (9, 2e-3) to (40, 2e-5); that is a slope of about 3.1, consistent with the label.

terms.meaning: The kinetic energy per unit wavenumber. Integrating it over all k gives the total energy. It is the distribution of energy over scales, with large scales at small k.
Spatial frequency: k = 2 pi divided by a length. A wave of wavelength lambda has k = 2 pi / lambda.
Half the mean square vorticity. In 2D flow it is a second inviscid invariant beside energy.
The transfer of energy or enstrophy between wavenumbers by nonlinear interaction. The flux Pi(k) is the net rate at which it crosses wavenumber k.
In 2D turbulence energy moves toward larger scales (smaller k) while enstrophy moves to smaller scales.
The mean square of the velocity difference between two points a distance r apart. It is a real-space way of looking at scale.
R(r) is the correlation of a fluctuation with itself at separation r, normalised to 1 at r = 0. The integral length scale is its area up to the first zero: the size of the energy-containing eddies.
A model of the effect of unresolved scales on resolved ones. The Smagorinsky model adds an eddy viscosity proportional to the local strain rate and the square of the filter width.
Rare strong events that make the tails of increment PDFs wider than a Gaussian at small separations.

remember: Energy is the area under E(k) against k on linear axes, but on log-log axes areas are not readable; use k E(k) against log k for that.
In 3D, the inertial range has E(k) proportional to k^(-5/3); in the 2D enstrophy range it is steeper, k^(-3). The reference slope must match the dimensionality.
A smooth field has S2(r) proportional to r^2 at small r. The r^(2/3) law belongs to the 3D inertial range, not to smooth scales.
The area under R(r) up to its first zero is the integral scale. A negative tail means the field has large-scale anti-correlation.
A Gaussian PDF has flatness 3; fat tails are flatness above 3.
A spectrum from one snapshot is noisy; a slope claim needs a window and an error bar.

understand.title: Five views of one distribution
understand.text: E(k) works in wavenumber space. S2(r) and R(r) are its real-space siblings: they carry the same second-order information, one as a function of scale, the other as a function of separation. The premultiplied spectrum k E(k) is E(k) re-weighted so that area under it against log k is energy. The flux Pi(k) adds the direction of transfer, which the slope never shows. The increment PDF goes beyond second order: it asks whether strong events are more frequent than a Gaussian would predict.

understand.title: What the null results mean
understand.text: The group includes two honest negative findings: the structure function departs from a clean power law, and the increment PDFs fall onto the Gaussian. Read them as limits of the data (one smooth, strongly damped 2D snapshot) rather than as statements about turbulence. A figure that fails to show the textbook feature is still informative when the reason is stated.

understand.title: Why the spectrum shows modelling quality
understand.text: An explicit sub-grid model removes energy near the grid cut-off. The test of a model is therefore not a global number but the shape of the last decade of resolved wavenumbers: with no model, energy piles up there; with a good model the curve bends down smoothly onto the reference.

steps.title: Energy is an integral of the spectrum
steps.note: Equal areas under the premultiplied curve k E(k), plotted against ln k, are equal energies. That is why its peak shows the energy-containing scale directly and why the 2D figure's peak sits at low k.

steps.title: Why the 2D enstrophy range has slope minus three
steps.note: Assume the spectrum in the range depends only on the enstrophy flux and on k. Check units: eta to the 2/3 gives T^-2, k^-3 gives L^3, so the product has the units of E(k). Dimensional analysis fixes the form; the constant C is empirical. Compare with the 3D energy range, where the same argument with the energy flux gives k^(-5/3).

steps.title: The flux and what its sign means
steps.note: T is the nonlinear transfer, which integrates to zero over all k. Pi(k) is the net rate at which energy arrives at wavenumbers above k. Positive means a forward (to small scales) transfer, negative means an inverse one. Sign conventions differ between authors; the legend of the figure fixes which is which.

steps.title: A smooth field has S2 proportional to r squared
steps.note: Taylor expansion for separations small compared with the smallest eddies. The log-log slope is 2, not 2/3. In the structure-function figure the curve is steepest at small r and bends over toward the 2/3 line only at larger r, so the reference line is not a test that the field has an inertial range.

steps.title: Structure function from the spectrum
steps.note: Both follow from the Wiener-Khinchin relation between a correlation and a spectrum along one line (E_1 is the one-dimensional spectrum). They are the same information as E(k), not independent evidence. S2 = 2 <u^2> (1 - R) when R is normalised.

steps.title: Integral length scale
steps.note: Truncating at the first zero is the usual practical cut on a finite periodic domain, where the tail of R is not reliable. The result is a measure of the largest energetic eddies and can be compared with the forcing or initial-condition scale.

steps.title: Gaussian reference for increments
steps.note: After scaling each separation's increments by their own standard deviation, one parameter-free curve is left. Peak 0.399, and at three standard deviations p is 0.0044. Flatness above 3 means fatter tails.

worked.title: Integral scale from the correlation curve, by trapezoid
worked.problem: Read from the correlation figure: R is 1.00 at r = 0, 0.81 at 0.25, 0.545 at 0.50, 0.31 at 0.75, 0.15 at 1.00, 0.045 at 1.25 and 0 at about 1.40. Estimate the area up to the first zero and compare with the legend value.

solution.text: Apply the trapezoid rule on each interval of width 0.25.
Add the last partial interval, from 1.25 to 1.40.

worked.answer: About 0.59, matching the legend value 0.588 to the precision of the read-off values.

analyze.q: The coarse curves are about 60 times higher than the reference at k = 1. List two explanations that involve normalisation and one that involves physics, and say which diagnostic separates them.
analyze.hint: Compute the total energy of each run directly from the velocity field and compare it with the area under E(k).

analyze.q: The structure-function slope is close to 2 at small r and flattens by r of about 20. What does that say about the smallest scale in the field, and why is the r^(2/3) reference line a weak test here?
analyze.hint: The Taylor argument above; the correlation function is also smooth near r = 0.

analyze.q: The flux is negative at low k and positive at high k. Which cascade does each sign represent, and why can the slope of E(k) not tell you?
analyze.hint: The spectrum is a magnitude; the flux is a signed rate.

evaluate.q: Is one snapshot of one run enough to say a closure 'does useful work'? State what the minimum defensible statement is, and what extra runs would turn it into a general claim.
evaluate.hint: Ensembles of initial conditions, Reynolds numbers, and a held-out resolution.

evaluate.q: The increment PDFs coincide with a Gaussian. Is that evidence that the flow lacks intermittency? Give two reasons it is not.
evaluate.hint: 2D versus 3D, strong damping by the model, and short samples that cannot resolve probabilities below about one in a thousand.

create: Redraw the spectrum figure so that the coarse and fine runs share one stated normalisation, the grid cut-off is marked with a vertical line, and the fit window of the dotted slope is shaded.
Design a one-page comparison panel that shows E(k), the flux Pi(k) and the increment flatness for the same snapshot, with a shared k axis where it applies.

checks.q: Why is a premultiplied spectrum plotted against log k used to find the energy-containing scale?
checks.hint: What is k E(k) d(ln k)?
checks.answer: Because k E(k) d(ln k) equals E(k) dk, so area under the premultiplied curve on a log axis is energy, and the peak marks the scale holding the most energy per logarithmic band. On a plain log-log E(k) plot, areas are distorted and the peak is hard to see.

checks.q: A spectrum falls from 2e-3 at k = 9 to 2e-5 at k = 40. What power-law exponent does that correspond to?
checks.hint: Use the log of the ratio over the log of the ratio of wavenumbers.
checks.answer: p = ln(100) / ln(40/9) = 4.605 / 1.492, about 3.1, consistent with a k^-3 range.

checks.q: The no-model coarse curve rises toward the last resolved wavenumber. What physical process is missing?
checks.hint: Where does energy go when it cascades past the grid?
checks.answer: Removal of enstrophy and energy at unresolved scales. With no sub-grid dissipation, the cascade is blocked at the grid cut-off and the transferred amount accumulates in the last resolved wavenumbers.

checks.q: Three increment PDFs at different separations all match a Gaussian. Your colleague says this proves the closure suppresses intermittency. Respond.
checks.hint: What else could cause the same picture?
checks.answer: It does not prove that. The sample is a single smooth, strongly damped 2D snapshot, the tails are noisy below about 1e-3, and 2D flows are not expected to show the 3D tail widening anyway. Only a test on a flow where the tails are known to be non-Gaussian, with and without the model, would address the claim.

checks.q: How would you test whether a coarse-grid difference in E(k) is a normalisation artefact?
checks.hint: A conservation check that does not depend on plotting.
checks.answer: Compute the total kinetic energy directly as the grid mean of u squared over two, for both runs, and compare it with the numerical integral of each plotted spectrum. The two must agree for each run; if the integral differs by a resolution-dependent factor, the plotted E(k) uses an unnormalised transform.
